title: Trajan’s Column is 100 Roman feet tall, said to be the height of a hill dug away for it
body: Trajan’s Column was dedicated in AD 113 in the new forum of Emperor Trajan, who ruled from 98 to 117; by his death the Roman Empire had reached its greatest extent. The column is 100 Roman feet (29.8 m) tall on a 5.4 m base, a hollow shaft with a spiral stair inside. The inscription over its door says it was set up *ad declarandum quantae altitudinis mons et locus tantis operibus sit egestus*: to show how high a hill and site were dug away for such great works. The historian Cassius Dio, writing about a century later, says the site had been hilly and Trajan cut it down by the column’s height. But geology, and digs of the early 1900s that found a street and houses of the early empire under the column’s foundation, showed that no such ridge stood there. The least unsatisfactory explanation, wrote [Platner and Ashby’s dictionary](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Gazetteer/Places/Europe/Italy/Lazio/Roma/Rome/_Texts/PLATOP*/Forum_Trajani.html) in 1929, is Christian Hülsen’s: the slope of the Quirinal Hill was cut back until the cut stood about 100 feet high, and **Trajan’s Markets** were built against it to hold it up. When Trajan died in 117, his ashes were laid in the base.

slides.question: Trajan’s Column in Rome is 100 Roman feet tall, not counting its base. About how many metres is that?
slides.explanation: About 29.8 m: a Roman foot was just under 30 cm. On its 5.4 m base the column stands about 35 m high.

slides.alt: Animation in cross-section at dusk: Trajan's Column with a gold ruler of 100 Roman feet, its base inscription, a ridge of earth dug away, a trench showing a Roman street under the column, then the Quirinal slope cut back to a face as tall as the column, with Trajan's Markets built against it.
slides.music: “Crusade - Heavy Industry” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Cut the hillside back to level ground. On a 30° slope, how far back must you dig for a face as tall as Trajan’s Column, 100 Roman feet?
slides.takeaway: About 52 m back, removing some 770 m³ of earth for every metre along the hill. Twice as high a face means four times the earth: a 100-foot cut was a vast job.

slides.alt: Photo of the lower half of Trajan’s Column in Rome: a marble shaft wrapped in a spiral band of carved figures, on a square base carved with weapons, with a small door and the inscription panel above it; broken grey granite columns of Trajan’s Forum stand in front.
slides.caption: Trajan’s Column today, behind granite columns of Trajan’s Forum. The inscription is the panel over the door in its base.

slides.text: For that entire section had been hilly and he had cut it down for a distance equal to the height of the column
slides.attribution: Cassius Dio, Roman History 68.16, early 200s AD (tr. Earnest Cary)

left.label: The old reading
left.text: A ridge 100 Roman feet high once filled the whole site, and the column marks how tall it was.

right.label: The likely reading
right.text: The slope of the Quirinal Hill beside the forum was cut back about 100 feet high, and Trajan’s Markets hold up the cut.

events.text: Trajan dies; ashes in the base.
A bronze St Peter replaces Trajan’s lost statue.

slides.question: What did digs in the early 1900s find under the foundation of Trajan’s Column in Rome?
slides.explanation: A street and houses of the early empire, so no hill stood on that spot. The ‘hill’ was most likely the cut-back slope of the Quirinal.
